summary:
Silent Monuments is an interactive 3D educational experience built in Unity by Judith Castillo Moreno, Marisa Méndez Mesén and Carolina Vargas Hidalgo. It centers on the Apollo 11 Lunar Module, Eagle, and was designed from an industrial design and user-centered pedagogical perspective.

The journey begins with an introduction to the mission’s context and the logic of modular spacecraft. Then, in a 3D lunar environment, users rebuild the Eagle by snapping four components into place: the Descent Stage, the Landing Gear and Ladder, the Ascent Stage, and the Communications and Radar Array. Each module unlocks a card explaining the engineering solutions and scientific discoveries linked to it. Once assembly is complete, a sequence simulates the historic stage separation and leads to a present-day view with NSSDCA records of what still remains on the Moon.

The project turns space history, often presented through static text and dense archives, into active, spatial learning. It matters because it preserves knowledge from past missions as humanity prepares to return to the Moon and head toward Mars, and because it gives young people, overwhelmed by fragmented information, a space to slow down and truly understand. It was also the team’s first hackathon, requiring them to combine industrial design, 3D optimization, UI/UX, and game engine integration.
details:
Silent Monuments

An interactive 3D educational assembly experience by:

Judith Castillo Moreno, Marisa Méndez Mesén and Carolina Vargas Hidalgo 

What did we develop? 

An interactive 3D educational assembly experience built in Unity centered on the Apollo 11 Lunar Module (Eagle). Designed from an industrial design and user-centered pedagogical perspective, the application guides users through a structured, narrative-driven journey from historical context to hands-on spacecraft construction and present-day preservation:

  • Mission Onboarding & Context: Users begin by exploring the core premise of modular spaceflight, understanding why spacecraft are engineered as sacrificial, multi-stage systems designed to fulfill specific phases of a mission.
  • Interactive 3D Modular Assembly: Inside a 3D lunar environment, users actively reconstruct the Eagle module by selecting and snapping four core structural components into place: the Descent Stage (octagonal base and braking engine), the Landing Gear and Ladder (telescopic shock-absorbing struts and footpads), the Ascent Stage (the pressurized crew cabin), and the Communications & Radar Array (S-band steerable antenna and rendezvous radar).
  • Progressive Engineering & Science Insights: As each module locks into place, an interactive card reveals concise insights explaining how engineers solved lunar challenges, alongside the scientific discoveries each component enabled.
  • Historical Stage Separation & Legacy View: Once the spacecraft is fully assembled, an interactive sequence simulates the historical departure from the lunar surface. Users watch the Ascent Stage lift off while the Descent Stage remains behind on the lunar surface, transitioning to a present-day archival view complete with NSSDCA mission records showing what still rests on the Moon today.

How does it address the challenge? 

Rather than presenting space exploration history through static text, dense archives, or passive timelines, our solution transforms spacecraft architecture into an active, spatial learning experience. By deconstructing a landmark spacecraft into functional modules, users connect industrial engineering decisions directly with historical and scientific outcomes.

Why is it important?

As humanity prepares to return to the Moon and venture further toward Mars and deep space, remembering where we came from is essential. History teaches us not only what is possible, but what past missions sacrificed, engineered, and discovered so we do not repeat past mistakes or lose the foundational knowledge that made spaceflight possible. At the same time, younger generations today are exposed to an overwhelming stream of fast-paced, fragmented information every single day, where they are often consuming facts passively without truly retaining or understanding them. Our project addresses this gap by offering an immersive, digital experience where students can slow down, build the Eagle on their own, and genuinely understand what humanity learned from our Moon and why the artifacts left behind on other worlds represent irreplaceable off-world cultural heritage.

Additionally, as first-time participants in a hackathon of this scale, building a complete 3D interactive prototype under tight time constraints pushed our team to bridge industrial design, 3D optimization, UI/UX, and game engine integration, demonstrating how interdisciplinary design thinking can turn complex aerospace history into accessible educational tools.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) 

During the preparation of our project, we utilized Google Gemini strictly as a workflow organization, technical guidance, and educational reference tool. Specifically, it helped us structure our team schedule, troubleshoot 3D mesh separation and FBX export workflows in Blender, understand basic C# object-snapping logic in Unity, and verify historical mission parameters. All 3D model preparation, PBR material assignment, rendering, UI/UX design, Unity scene integration, and pitch materials were created and executed directly by our team.

Third-Party Assets & Data Credits:

  • 3D Base Model: "Apollo 11 Lunar Module - 1969" by NINATOR (https://skfb.ly/oJFFu), licensed under Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), separated into modular components and textured with custom PBR materials and lunar terrain by our team.
  • Scientific & Historical Data: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) and Apollo 11 Mission Reports.
